clue.text: Yours truly, a devil in disguise, very old

indicators.note: something in disguise has had its appearance altered, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to being an ancient devil masquerading in human form.
explanation.definitionFit: The Middle Ages lie centuries back, so anything from that period is loosely described as very ancient.

clue.text: Gifts editor's received an indication of the value of good company

definitions.text: an indication of the value of good company

indicators.note: the phrase has taken in, or received, the letters that make up the answer

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A newspaper's gifts editor has been sent a guide to which companies make good presents.
explanation.walkthrough: The FTSE 100 is the London stock market index of leading companies; 'good company' is a playful way of saying blue-chip firms.
explanation.definitionFit: A share index measures the market worth of major listed firms, tracking how well they are doing.

clue.text: Discovered seaside town's fine

indicators.note: dis-covered means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters go

blocks.note: the resort on England's south coast

explanation.surface: A seaside resort has been found to be perfectly pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: Brighton is a seaside town on England's south coast; remove its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words of agreement, as in replying 'okay' to a suggestion.

clue.text: Wobbling perhaps, finally offer a parting expression of affection

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word that follows it
parting an expression splits it open so something can be placed in the gap

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
as in 'bless him!', a fond exclamation

explanation.surface: Someone, perhaps unsteadily, offers a fond farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair from 'finally offer a' go into the split expression of affection. The definition is cheeky: going without support may result in wobbling.
explanation.definitionFit: Going without a bra leaves the bust unsupported, so wobbling is an example of what might be seen.

clue.text: Sailor, head of college before Oxford, from Shimla initially, on the wagon

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter
initially points to the opening letter of the town named before it

blocks.note: an old word for a farm wagon

explanation.surface: A sailor who went to an Oxford college and then India has given up drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the wagon' looks like the idiom for teetotal, but the wagon is simply WAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The cox who steers a ship's boat is a member of the crew, so a type of seaman.

clue.text: An elegant chest that is right to cover with transparent silk

explanation.surface: An instruction to drape sheer silk over a fine piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the fabric sits on top of, covering, the abbreviations below it.
explanation.definitionFit: A chiffonier is a tall ornamental cabinet or chest of drawers, a fine piece of furniture.

clue.text: Go first on Stephenson's Rocket, say?

indicators.note: the first on a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A question about travelling first class on the famous early steam locomotive.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephenson's Rocket was a pioneering steam engine, but rocket here is the peppery salad green.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocket, also called arugula, is a salad plant eaten for its foliage, so it is an example of this.

clue.text: It's behind Brighton Rock partners introducing odd stripe

indicators.note: odd means strange or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: you and I together, a pair of partners; also West and East at bridge
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something lies behind a stick of the famous seaside candy, with a couple bringing in an odd stripe.
explanation.walkthrough: Brighton Rock is both a seaside sweet and a Graham Greene novel; the West Pier, now a ruin, stands on the Brighton seafront, behind the shops selling rock.
explanation.definitionFit: The West Pier is a landmark of the Brighton seafront, the setting associated with the town's famous sweet.

clue.text: Roe stripped, see her bouncing around for Hugh, reportedly?

indicators.note: stripping a word removes its outer layer, keeping only the centre
letters bouncing around are jumbled into a new order
reportedly signals that the name is to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: the letter's name is pronounced like the verb

explanation.surface: A cook strips fish eggs and watches a woman leap about, apparently for someone called Hugh.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is itself a sound-alike: Hugh said out loud is 'hue', and the answer is a hue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is a yellowish-brown earth pigment and the colour named after it, so it is a shade.

clue.text: Radio device's error, dropping station

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so those letters are removed

explanation.surface: A radio has made a mistake and lost its station.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove STA from the middle of the word for an error.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike is short for microphone, the instrument broadcasters speak into on air.

clue.text: Lavishly, all over the place, old female entertained in academia

indicators.note: something all over the place is in disorder, so the letters are scrambled
a host entertains guests inside, so these letters are taken in

explanation.surface: An elderly woman was lavishly entertained at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: The two abbreviations join the adverb's letters before all are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy-covered buildings symbolise old universities, so the phrase is a nickname for the scholarly world.

clue.text: In position of authority, crossword supremo ultimately gets to excel

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letters of the two words before it

blocks.note: in charge of, as in over the staff
the last letter of each word

explanation.surface: Someone who rules the crossword world finally gets the chance to shine.
explanation.walkthrough: Excel is used in its older sense of surpassing or going beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel in the archaic sense is to exceed, and to overdo is to go beyond what is needed.

clue.text: Winchester maybe with scope to get used here?

definitions.text: Winchester maybe with scope to get used here?

blocks.note: a Winchester is a make of gun

explanation.surface: A question about where a telescopic-sighted Winchester gets practised with.
explanation.walkthrough: Winchester looks like the English cathedral city, but it is the American gun maker; the whole clue also describes the place.
explanation.definitionFit: A shooting range is the facility where marksmen practise firing guns, including Winchesters fitted with scopes.

clue.text: Unlikely case, drier beach

indicators.note: an unlikely version of a word is an improbable rearrangement of it

blocks.note: an oast is a kiln for drying hops

explanation.surface: An improbable argument that a beach could be less damp.
explanation.walkthrough: Oast houses, with their distinctive cowled roofs, are a feature of Kent's hop country.
explanation.definitionFit: The shore where land meets the ocean is the seacoast, and a beach is part of it.

clue.text: Amid racket cancel Bristol City's suspension

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one word goes inside the other

explanation.surface: Amid controversy, a football club's player ban is overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol City is a football club, so 'suspension' suggests a ban, but it is the Clifton Suspension Bridge over the Avon Gorge in Bristol.
explanation.definitionFit: Clifton names the famous suspension bridge in the city of Bristol, so it identifies the city's suspension.

clue.text: A glass, old boy, is to be raised to Diana shortly

indicators.note: raising letters in a down entry reads them upwards, back to front
shortly means cut short, so the name loses its last letter

explanation.surface: An old school pal proposes a toast to someone called Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A glass' sounds like a drink to be raised in a toast; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsidian is a dark natural glass formed when volcanic lava cools quickly.

clue.text: 501 advanced into pub, heading for alcoholic state

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the number goes within the pub
the heading of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: a synonym, split around the inserted letters
Roman numerals D for 500 and I for 1

explanation.surface: Someone advanced into a bar heading for a drunken condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alcoholic state' suggests drunkenness, but the state is a US one.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Bundles of joy in cheeky couple, wrinkly one on top

indicators.note: something wrinkly is creased out of shape, so the word's letters are crumpled

blocks.note: the buttocks, a pair of cheeks

explanation.surface: Babies in a couple's care, with an old person keeping watch over them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrinkly' looks like a slang noun for an old person but is the anagram signal; in a down entry 'on top' puts the rearranged word first.
explanation.definitionFit: Newborn babies are proverbially bundles of joy, and neonates is the medical word for newborns.

clue.text: Stage at which, sadly, Hugh's retirement starts – no chicken!

indicators.note: starts points to the opening letters of the two words before it
sadly means badly, things going wrong, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: a stage of a journey or race

explanation.surface: The setter Hugo laments the moment of retirement when he is no longer young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At which' only links the parts. 'No chicken' recalls 'no spring chicken', but the chicken is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leghorn is a breed of domestic fowl, named after the Italian port also known as Livorno.

clue.text: Film-maker entices strangely accommodating adult

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd way, so the letters are arranged oddly
accommodating means housing a guest, so a letter is taken inside

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as in film certificates

explanation.surface: A director lures a grown-up in a strange, obliging way.
explanation.definitionFit: A cineaste is a devotee of cinema, a word also used for those who make films.

clue.text: A peddler of ecstasy was I, legendary lover of Ireland

blocks.note: a peddler is someone who sold things

explanation.surface: A confession from someone who once dealt drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the confession as 'I sold E'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolde is the Irish princess in the Arthurian tale of Tristan and Isolde, famed for her tragic romance.

clue.text: Busted singer in country performing following split

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the second piece named is placed first

explanation.surface: A singer is arrested in some country while performing after a breakup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busted' suggests arrested; it means bosomy. Dolly Parton is a country music star.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolly Parton is a famously buxom singer in country music, as she herself often jokes.

clue.text: Always centrally located, Hispanic canal's dramatic – here?

definitions.text: Always centrally located, Hispanic canal's dramatic – here?

indicators.note: always tells you to apply the central rule to every following word, keeping the middle pair each time

blocks.note: the middle two letters, counting the s

explanation.surface: A question about where a Latin American canal sits at the centre and makes an impact.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the country: it is in the centre of the Americas, Spanish-speaking, and its canal is impressive.
explanation.definitionFit: Panama is the Central American, Spanish-speaking country through which the famous canal is cut.

clue.text: What one might read about in History Today sometimes

definitions.text: What one might read about in History Today

blocks.clueFragment: What one might read about in History Today
blocks.note: the setter's reading: history covers then, today covers now

explanation.surface: A reader of a history magazine finds some articles there occasionally.
explanation.walkthrough: History Today is a British history magazine; split it into its two words for the two time periods.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means occasionally, and literally pairs the present with the past.

clue.text: In James, a uniquely hairy man

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the name, the article and the start of the adverb

explanation.surface: Someone named James is described as exceptionally hirsute.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Jacob's twin is described as a hairy man; James is a book of the Bible too, adding to the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis calls the elder twin of Jacob a hairy man, contrasting him with his smooth brother.

clue.text: Pickle, just flip the lid up, girl!

indicators.note: up in a down entry means the word is read from bottom to top
flipping off the lid removes it from the top of the jar

blocks.note: a tricky situation, as in being in a pickle

explanation.surface: Someone urges a girl to just open a jar of pickle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickle' looks like a jarred relish but means a predicament; the opening of that word matches the lid written upwards, so remove it.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is a common girl's name, and crosswords freely define first names this way.

clue.text: Setter say needing master, and principles laid down

blocks.note: a setter is a breed of dog

explanation.surface: A crossword setter needs an expert, and sets out the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter suggests the crossword compiler; here it is the gun dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogma is a set of beliefs laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true.

clue.text: Have a flashback of free unclothed Johnson

indicators.note: unclothed means stripped of its outer covering, leaving only the inside

blocks.note: slang for the male organ, as is johnson

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a naked politician named Johnson running free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Johnson' suggests Boris or Samuel, but it is slang for a penis, as is member.
explanation.definitionFit: To remember an event is to recall it, as a flashback brings a past scene back to mind.
